records.cause: Git Bash (MSYS2) automatically translates POSIX paths to Windows paths. `/mnt/c/Users/...` becomes `C:/Program Files/Git/mnt/c/Users/...`. This happens because MSYS2 sees `/mnt/c/` as a POSIX path and prepends its own installation prefix.
records.remedy: Add `MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL=/mnt` prefix to all WSL commands run from Git Bash. If robocopy is involved, use `MSYS2_ENV_CONV_EXCL='*' cmd.exe //c "robocopy ..."`.
records.symptom: Commands like `wsl -d Ubuntu-26.04 -u root bash /mnt/c/Users/.../script.sh` fail with:
records.title: MSYS2 Path Translation Breaks WSL Commands from Git Bash

records.cause: `apt_pkg` issue: Python 3.14t replaces system Python, breaking apt's Python bindings. Fix: `apt install --reinstall python3-apt` before `apt update`. 2. `libdb-dev` renamed in Ubuntu 26.04 (Resolute): `libdb-dev` → `libdb5.3-dev`. Python build doesn't need Berkeley DB — it's optional and can be skipped. 3. Intel GPU repo targets `noble` (24.04), not `resolute` (26.04). Must be skipped until Intel adds 26.04 support.
records.remedy: When writing distro-specific scripts, check package names with `apt-cache search` first. Always handle optional dependencies with `|| warn` to avoid `set -e` aborting the script.
records.symptom: Post-install script on Ubuntu 26.04 fails with: - `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'apt_pkg'` during `apt update` - `libdb-dev` package not installable - Intel GPU drivers not installable (wrong Ubuntu release)
records.title: Python 3.14t Source Build on Ubuntu 26.04 (apt_pkg + libdb)

records.cause: A previous assistant incorrectly concluded that `autoflake v2.3.3` "crashes" on Python 3.14t free-threading. This was a false diagnosis — autoflake is a pure-Python tool (depends only on `pyflakes`, no C extensions) and works correctly on 3.14t.

records.remedy: Before declaring ANY tool "broken on 3.14t", isolate the failure mode: - Test the tool directly in Python: `python -c "import subprocess; ..."` - Run `python -m autoflake --version` to confirm it loads - Check if it's a C-extension package (needs cp314t wheel) or pure-Python (works everywhere) 2. Pure-Python tools (autoflake, pyflakes, isort, black, ruff) work on 3.14t — they have no C extensions that need recompilation 3. Only C-extension packages (psutil, pydantic-core, numpy, psycopg2) need cp314t wheel verification 4. If a tool fails via basher/subprocess, suspect shell escaping before 3.14t incompatibility
records.symptom: on Python 3.14t free-threading. This was a false diagnosis — autoflake is a pure-Python tool (depends only on `pyflakes`, no C extensions) and works correctly on 3.14t.

records.cause: Git Bash (MSYS2) shell interprets `$`, `{`, `}`, `%`, and pipe characters BEFORE they reach PowerShell. Multi-line PowerShell commands with string interpolation and format operators get mangled by the shell layer.
records.remedy: For any PowerShell command with `$`, `{`, `}`, `|`, or `%`: write to `.ps1` file first 2. Keep PowerShell one-liners to single commands without variable interpolation 3. Use Python pathlib instead of PowerShell for file operations when possible 4. Test the command standalone in PowerShell before putting it in basher

records.cause: Git Bash (MSYS2) treats `\` as an escape character, not a path separator. `\U` (from `C:\Users`) is interpreted as a literal `U`, and `\D` (from `Desktop`) is interpreted as a literal `D`. The path `C:\Users\clint\Desktop` becomes `C:UsersclintDesktop`.
records.remedy: Prefer Python pathlib for all file operations in scripts 2. When using shell commands, use forward slashes 3. Never pass Windows backslash paths directly to bash commands 4. For `cmd.exe` commands, use `cmd.exe //c` prefix to bypass MSYS2 translation
records.symptom: Commands with Windows backslash paths fail silently or produce expected results:
records.title: Windows Backslash Path Interpretation in Git Bash

records.cause: Introduced `yield from _safe_walk(search_path)` into the function body. Python treats any function containing `yield` as a generator function. Callers (`run_full_test` does `files[:50]`) expected `List[str]` but received a generator object — slicing would TypeError. The `_safe_walk` inner function correctly collected files via side-effect `append()`, but the outer function's `yield from` made it return a generator instead of the accumulated list.
records.remedy: Do not introduce `yield`/`yield from` into functions that callers expect to return concrete types. Verify caller expectations (list slicing, len(), iteration patterns) before converting to generator.

records.title: Generator-vs-List Bug in TARBABY discover_python_files()

records.cause: All three SQLite connection points used `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE`. Under concurrent writes from multiple memory systems (DirectMemory + LocalMemoryStore + MemoryBus), the second writer gets `sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked`.

records.cause: When PAMS is unreachable, MemoryBus stores messages in an in-memory Python list (`self._local_queue`). On process exit, ALL messages are permanently lost. No SQLite, no JSON file, no disk persistence.

records.cause: `ClusterWORMZ.execute_all()` uses `FreeThreadPool` (built on `ThreadPoolExecutor`) to run worms in parallel. Worker threads call `_resolve_worm_dynamic()` which calls `discover_worms()` → `importlib.import_module()`. Under Python 3.14t free-threading (no GIL), `importlib.import_module()` is NOT thread-safe — concurrent imports from multiple worker threads can deadlock the import system.
records.date: June 3, 2026 — while writing parallel integration tests
records.remedy: Never call `importlib.import_module()` or `discover_worms()` from background threads - Pre-initialize all lazy singletons (registry, breaker, config) on the main thread before entering thread pools - Use module-level imports for frequently-used modules in threaded code — function-body imports are a deadlock risk under 3.14t - Use `FreeThreadPool.shutdown(wait=False)` — the caller is responsible for draining futures via `as_completed()` - Test threaded code on both GIL and free-threaded Python (the deadlock only manifests under 3.14t)

records.cause: The original `discover_worms()` used `split(os.sep)[-1]` to extract filenames for the pre-computed `registered_files` set. records.cause: `freebuff.exe` was compiled with Bun v1.3.11 on Windows. Bun's JavaScript engine (JavaScriptCore from WebKit) uses custom memory allocators (`bmalloc` and `libpas`) that are NOT stable on Windows. These allocators cause segmentation faults (access violation 0xc0000005, SIGSEGV exit 139) during GC cycles, memory pressure, or worker IPC in standalone compiled binaries.
records.date: June 4, 2026 — Bun crash investigation session
records.remedy: Always compile standalone binaries with latest Bun (1.3.14+ for Windows) - Set up WER crash dumps for all Bun-compiled production binaries - Use ProcDump monitoring during testing and development - Never ship Bun v1.3.11 or earlier standalone binaries on Windows - Check oven-sh/bun GitHub issues for Windows stability before deploying

records.symptom: `sentinel_enforcer` gates file writes with `_GATED_CALL = threading.local()`. The permit is granted on whichever thread happens to ask. `fs_probe` then runs its child probe on a new worker thread and opens a temp file there — so once the guard was armed, every delegated probe failed, and the API returned `None`. `None` means "unknown", so the caller could not tell "blocked by our own security control" from "the path did not answer".
records.title: Lesson #91 — "I Permitted It" Is Not a Process-Wide Fact: Per-Thread State Gates Are Invisible Until a Worker Runs

records.symptom: `orchestrate(max_natures=1)` ran zero Natures and reported `phase="complete"`. The cap was applied to a ranked list, and a filter one step later could delete the very item the cap had just paid for:
records.title: Lesson #92 — A Cap Applied Before a Filter Is a Cap on Nothing, and "Complete" Must Not Be Reachable With an Empty Record

records.symptom: A triage wrote `evidence` only in the branch that moved a row from `pending` to `dispatched`. The table is regenerated by re-running the tool, so the second run saw `dispatched`, skipped the branch, and produced 62 decisions with no locations. Nothing consumed the field except a contract test, so the loss was silent for as long as that test was failing for another reason.
records.title: Lesson #93 — A Measurement Written Inside a Transition Is a Cache With No Rebuild Path

records.symptom: The isolation fixture that repaired Error #196 recomputed each module's DB-path global from the environment. But two test modules redirect that global deliberately, to a path the environment does not describe -- so the repair replaced their redirect with the shared session store after the first test.
records.title: Lesson #94 — A Repair That Recomputes the Old Value Is Not a Restore; It Is a Second Leak

records.symptom: Three assertions failed together in the aggregate run and none of them was about the code: a 3.112s call against a 3.0s "probable deadlock" bound, two `overdue()` polls whose clock-derived `overdue_by` read 0.020 then 0.021, and a benchmark whose 2-worker run beat its 1-worker run by less than nothing. All three passed alone. All three were reading contention.
records.title: Lesson #95 — A Wall-Clock Assertion on a Shared Machine Grades the Machine

records.symptom: `wire_or_cut` rebuilt every declaration from four hand-picked keys, so a plain `--verdict` run dropped `evidence` (and `triage`). `--propose` had been fixed for the same field the day before, and the suite went green -- because the file that test run produced was written *with* `--propose`. The refresh path does not pass `--propose`, so the next refresh rewrote 62 `dispatched` rows with 0 locations, and the contract test failed against an artifact nothing had edited by hand.
records.title: Lesson #96 — Regenerate an Artifact the Way the Refresh Path Regenerates It

records.symptom: The type gate keys each diagnostic as `path:line:col:rule`. Inserting lines above a finding changes the key, so a session that introduced no type defect reported 15 new diagnostics and 6 gone -- the six "new" ones were the six "gone" ones moved, and only reading both lists told you so. Nine of the fifteen were real and belonged to a different process's generated output under `_staging/`.
records.title: Lesson #97 — A Baseline Key That an Unrelated Edit Can Change Is Not an Identity

records.symptom: `nerve._LazyTorch` bounded a torch import with a 25 s join on a daemon thread and returned `timeout` when the join expired. On a contended box the expiry fired, the thread kept importing, and the half-built module in `sys.modules` was handed to the next `import torch` anywhere in the process: 25 torch tests failed with `partially initialized module 'torch' ... has no attribute 'distributed'`, in two separate long runs, while every uncontended run of the same suite was green.
records.title: Lesson #98 — A Bound You Enforce by Walking Away Is a Fork, Not a Bound

records.symptom: `test_mesh_html_view` failed with `ReferenceError: vis is not defined` because the generated artifact linked vis.js from unpkg and the box had no route there. The harness reported precisely what it saw; the defect was that *the check had inherited the artifact's dependency on the network*. A corpus scan then found 52 generated views in the same position (`unpkg`, `cdnjs`, `jsdelivr`) -- and only the mesh view has a verifier, so the other 51 fail silently wherever offline.
records.title: Lesson #99 — A Check Inherits Its Subject's Dependencies

records.symptom: The largest artifact in the repository was the one I trusted least, and I had the reason backwards. `graphify-out/graph.json` is 688,627 nodes over 51,186 files — so when 101 rows needed one question answered (*is this function reachable from production?*), it looked like the instrument to reach for. It is not. Asked `explain "create_backup"` it returned `bibl_c_create_backup`, a prose entry from `src/ORCHESTRATION/BIBL/C.md L8356`, degree 1. Asked who calls `DatabaseMonitorWorm.create_backup` it returned three nodes and no callers, having resolved the *name* to the bibliography stub and the *class* to the right file.

records.symptom: `scripts/graph_refresh_no_llm.py` hard-coded its graphify interpreter to the pip install in the system Python 3.14, and defended it in a comment: *"graphify lives in the system interpreter, not the venv. Hard-coded rather than inherited from `sys.executable` because inheriting it is the bug."* The premise is correct — the 3.14t venv has no graphify, so inheriting reaches nothing. The target is wrong, and the comment's confidence is what kept anyone from looking: that install is a flat package with no `exporters/`, so it cannot carry `scripts/graphify_node_limit_patch.py` (which rewrites `exporters/html.py`), and `graphify_huge_mode.py` — the renderer for 688k nodes — is read out of that ver…

records.symptom: I added a `declared_in_data` decider -- a wire that lives in JSON rather than Python, invisible to a name probe -- and it resolved 101 of 101 pending rows on the first run. On AIME25 with 32K-token generation it matches Full Attention accuracy at 2.5x throughput or 10.7x KV memory reduction; baselines keep only ~half accuracy at same efficiency.
records.title: Trigonometry fixes the AI memory bottleneck steal
